blocks.text: Nigeria has rewritten its rulebook more often than most students realise. Clifford in 1922 allowed four elected Nigerians. Lyttleton in 1954 made the country a federation. The 1963 Republic took the Queen out of the picture. Soldiers tore the book up in 1966, 1983 and 1993. The copy in force today is dated 1999. Constitutional development is that sequence — and the reasons each document was already out of date when it was signed.

blocks.title: Constitutional development
blocks.text: The process by which the rules of government in Nigeria have been made, replaced and restored — from colonial constitutions named after British governors and secretaries of state, through independence and the republics, including the interruptions of military rule.

rows: First elective principle: 3 seats for Lagos, 1 for Calabar; Legislative Council for the Colony and Southern Provinces only; North excluded; limited, property-based franchise; stimulated the NNDP
Brought the North into a central legislature; created three regional councils (North, East, West) — the start of regionalism; still a limited franchise and a strong official majority

House of Representatives; Council of Ministers with Nigerian ministers; regional Houses of Assembly (and Houses of Chiefs in North and West); wider though still incomplete franchise; drafted after more consultation than Richards
True federal constitution: exclusive and concurrent lists, residual powers to the regions, regional premiers, Lagos as federal territory; the structure that led to independence
blocks.caption: Colonial constitutions from Clifford to Lyttleton. Independence (1960) and the Republican Constitution (1963) follow this sequence

blocks.markdown:
### Independence and the four republics

The **Independence Constitution of 1960** retained the Queen as Head of State, represented by a Governor-General, with a Prime Minister (Tafawa Balewa) in a parliamentary system.

**First Republic, 1 October 1963.** The Republican Constitution replaced the Queen with a Nigerian President (Nnamdi Azikiwe) as ceremonial Head of State; Balewa remained Prime Minister. The republic was ended by the January 1966 coup.

**Second Republic, 1 October 1979.** The 1979 Constitution introduced an **executive presidential** system modelled on the United States: a President as Head of State and Head of Government (Shehu Shagari), a bicameral National Assembly, and 19 states. It was overthrown on 31 December 1983.

**Third Republic, 1993.** Babangida's transition produced a two-party contest (SDP and NRC) and the **12 June 1993** presidential election, widely regarded as won by M.K.O. Abiola. The election was annulled; the republic was aborted. An Interim National Government under Ernest Shonekan was swept aside by Sani Abacha.

**Fourth Republic, 29 May 1999.** The 1999 Constitution restored civilian presidential government over **36 states and the FCT**, with a National Assembly of **109 senators and 360 representatives**. It remains in force, as amended.

items: **From regions to states.** Three regions at independence; Mid-Western Region created in 1963; **12 states in 1967** (Gowon, during the crisis that became the civil war); 19 states in 1976; 21 in 1987; 30 in 1991; **36 states in 1996**, plus the FCT.

**Federalism** was adopted because of Nigeria's size, ethnic and cultural diversity, the need to allay **minority fears**, and the wish of each big group not to be ruled from a single regional capital of another group.
**Revenue allocation** has been a standing quarrel: derivation versus population versus equality of states; oil has intensified the fight between producing areas and the centre.
**State creation** was used to break regional monopolies and to answer minority demands, but it also multiplied overheads and new 'minorities' inside new states.
**Over-centralisation** in practice — especially under military rule and through federal control of oil revenue — sits in tension with the federal text of the 1999 Constitution.
**Indigene / settler** conflicts and agitation for more states and local governments remain unresolved problems of Nigerian federalism.

blocks.title: Parliamentary then presidential
blocks.text: 1960 and 1963 were parliamentary (Prime Minister as head of government). 1979 and 1999 are presidential (an executive President). Mixing those labels — calling Balewa a President, or Shagari a Prime Minister — is an immediate lost mark.

blocks.title: A timeline from Clifford to the Fourth Republic
blocks.prompt: Place the following on a single timeline and state what each changed: Clifford, Richards, Macpherson, Lyttleton, independence, First Republic, military interruption, Second Republic, aborted Third Republic, Fourth Republic.

steps.text: 1946 Richards — North included; three regions appear.
1954 Lyttleton — federation with legislative lists and regional premiers.
1960 independence — parliamentary, Queen as Head of State.
1963 First Republic — parliamentary, Nigerian President ceremonial.
1966–1979 military rule (with a civil war, 1967–1970, and 12 states in 1967).
1979 Second Republic — presidential; ended December 1983, then more military rule.
1999 Fourth Republic — presidential, 36 states + FCT, 109/360 legislature, still in force.

blocks.answer: Clifford 1922 → Richards 1946 → Macpherson 1951 → Lyttleton 1954 → independence 1960 → First Republic 1963 → military rule → Second Republic 1979 → military rule and aborted Third Republic 1993 → Fourth Republic 1999

blocks.title: Clifford is elective principle; Lyttleton is federalism
blocks.text: If you remember only two colonial tags, remember those. Richards = regionalism and the North in the centre. Macpherson = more Nigerian ministers and consultation. Republics: 1963, 1979, 1993 (aborted), 1999. Do not call 1960 the First Republic if the question follows WAEC's 1963 dating — independence and the republic are consecutive but not the same event.

points: Clifford 1922 introduced the elective principle in Lagos and Calabar; Richards 1946 created regionalism and included the North; Macpherson 1951 expanded Nigerian participation; Lyttleton 1954 established federalism.
Independence came on 1 October 1960 under a parliamentary constitution with the Queen as Head of State.
The four republics date from 1963 (First), 1979 (Second), 1993 (aborted Third) and 1999 (Fourth).
1960–66 was parliamentary; 1979 and 1999 are presidential. Military coups interrupted civilian rule in 1966, 1983 and after June 12 1993.
Nigerian federalism grew from three regions to 36 states and the FCT; its problems include revenue allocation, minority fears, state-creation agitation and over-centralisation.
